notes: See data/README.md for provenance rules. Every source_url was checked to resolve and to support its definition on 2026-10-16. source_url stays null where no public-domain source has been found yet.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Extra fat has built up inside the liver. This is a common finding and is often picked up by chance on a scan.
entries.clinical_context: Graded on imaging as mild, moderate, or severe. Frequently reported alongside liver enzyme results.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: ALT is an enzyme found mostly in the liver. A blood test measures how much of it is in your blood. Higher than usual levels can be a sign the liver is irritated.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in a liver function panel, usually next to AST. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: AST is an enzyme found in the liver and also in muscle. A blood test measures how much is in your blood.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in a liver function panel, usually paired with ALT.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: A blood test that shows your average blood sugar level over roughly the past three months, rather than just at the moment of the test.
entries.clinical_context: Reported as a percentage. Used to monitor blood sugar control over time.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Blood pressure that stays higher than the normal range over time.
entries.clinical_context: Recorded as two numbers, for example 140/90. Often tracked across several visits.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A hard deposit, like a small stone, that has formed inside the kidney.
entries.clinical_context: Size and location are usually described on imaging reports.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: One or more hard, stone-like lumps that have formed in the gallbladder.
entries.clinical_context: Commonly seen on abdominal ultrasound. May or may not cause symptoms.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: The heart looks larger than usual on a scan or X-ray.
entries.clinical_context: Often first noted on a chest X-ray, then looked at more closely with other tests.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A part of the lung has not filled with air the way it normally would, so that area looks flattened or closed on a scan.
entries.clinical_context: Often described by location and extent, for example 'basilar' meaning at the bottom of the lung.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Extra fluid has collected in the space between the lung and the chest wall.
entries.clinical_context: Usually described as small, moderate, or large, and on which side.
entries.source_citation: NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms - 'pleural effusion'

entries.label: SYMPTOM
entries.plain_definition: Swelling caused by extra fluid collecting in body tissue, often in the legs, ankles, or feet.
entries.clinical_context: Sometimes described as 'pitting' if pressing on the skin leaves a dent.

entries.label: SYMPTOM
entries.plain_definition: Difficulty breathing, or the feeling of not being able to get enough air.
entries.clinical_context: Often noted as happening at rest or only with activity, for example 'on exertion'.

entries.label: SYMPTOM
entries.plain_definition: A heartbeat that is faster than the usual resting rate.
entries.clinical_context: Measured in beats per minute. Many everyday things, such as exercise or anxiety, can raise heart rate.

entries.label: SYMPTOM
entries.plain_definition: A heartbeat that is slower than the usual resting rate.
entries.clinical_context: Measured in beats per minute. Can be normal in people who are very physically fit.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: A waste product your muscles make every day. The kidneys normally clear it out of the blood, so a blood test for it gives information about how the kidneys are working.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in a kidney function panel, usually alongside eGFR.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: A number that estimates how well your kidneys are filtering waste out of your blood. It is calculated from a blood test.
entries.clinical_context: Usually calculated from creatinine along with age and other factors.
entries.source_citation: MedlinePlus Medical Tests - 'Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR) and GFR Tests'

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: One of the types of cholesterol measured in a blood test. It is often called 'bad' cholesterol because higher levels are linked to fatty buildup in blood vessels.
entries.clinical_context: Reported as part of a lipid panel with HDL and triglycerides.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: One of the types of cholesterol measured in a blood test. It is often called 'good' cholesterol.
entries.clinical_context: Reported as part of a lipid panel with LDL and triglycerides.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: A type of fat carried in your blood, measured by a blood test.
entries.clinical_context: Reported as part of a lipid panel. Levels can be affected by what you ate before the test.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: The fats and cholesterol measured in your blood are outside the usual range.
entries.clinical_context: Based on the combined results of a lipid panel rather than a single number.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Having fewer red blood cells, or less hemoglobin in them, than usual. Red blood cells carry oxygen around your body.
entries.clinical_context: Identified from a full blood count. There are many different causes.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: The part of your red blood cells that carries oxygen. A blood test measures how much of it you have.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in a complete blood count (CBC). Normal ranges differ by age and sex.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A higher than usual number of white blood cells in your blood. White blood cells are part of how your body fights infection.
entries.clinical_context: Seen on a complete blood count. Has many possible causes.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A lower than usual number of platelets in your blood. Platelets are the cell fragments that help your blood clot.
entries.clinical_context: Seen on a complete blood count.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Bone density that is lower than usual, but not low enough to be called osteoporosis.
entries.clinical_context: Measured with a bone density scan and reported as a T-score.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A condition where bones become thinner and more fragile than usual, which makes them easier to break.
entries.clinical_context: Measured with a bone density scan and reported as a T-score.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Everyday wear-and-tear changes in the cushions between the bones of the spine. It is very common as people get older.
entries.clinical_context: Frequently reported on spine imaging, often as an incidental finding.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Age-related wear-and-tear changes in the bones and joints of the spine.
entries.clinical_context: Described by the region of the spine involved, for example lumbar (lower back) or cervical (neck).

entries.label: DESCRIPTOR
entries.plain_definition: Not cancerous.
entries.clinical_context: Used to describe growths, lumps, or findings that are not cancer.

entries.label: DESCRIPTOR
entries.plain_definition: A general word for an area of tissue that looks different from the tissue around it. It does not by itself say whether something is serious.
entries.clinical_context: Usually described further by size, location, and appearance.

entries.label: DESCRIPTOR
entries.plain_definition: A small rounded lump of tissue. The word describes the shape and size only, not whether it is harmful.
entries.clinical_context: Reports usually give the size in millimetres and where it is.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: The thyroid gland is making less thyroid hormone than the body usually needs.
entries.clinical_context: Usually identified from thyroid blood tests including TSH.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: A hormone measured by a blood test that shows how the thyroid gland is being signalled to work.
entries.clinical_context: Usually the first thyroid test ordered, sometimes with T3 and T4.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Stomach acid comes back up into the food pipe often enough to cause symptoms such as heartburn.
entries.clinical_context: Often diagnosed from symptoms; sometimes confirmed with endoscopy.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Irritation or inflammation of the lining of the stomach.
entries.clinical_context: May be described on an endoscopy report.

entries.label: TEST
entries.plain_definition: The heart's electrical pattern is following its normal path at a normal rate. This is the expected result on a heart tracing.
entries.clinical_context: Reported on an ECG (also written EKG).

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A heart attack. Blood flow to part of the heart muscle is blocked, so that part of the muscle is damaged.
entries.clinical_context: May be described as recent or previous. Often referenced in past medical history.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: An area of the body is not getting as much blood flow as it needs.
entries.clinical_context: Described by the organ involved, for example cardiac or cerebral.

entries.label: TEST
entries.plain_definition: Protein is showing up in your urine. Urine does not usually contain much protein.
entries.clinical_context: Found on a urine test, sometimes as part of checking kidney function.

entries.label: TEST
entries.plain_definition: A small amount of a protein called albumin is showing up in your urine, at a level too low to see on a standard urine test.
entries.clinical_context: Measured with a specific urine albumin test.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Urine has backed up and made part of the kidney swell.
entries.clinical_context: Usually graded as mild, moderate, or severe on imaging.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: The liver is larger than usual.
entries.clinical_context: Measured on imaging, often reported in centimetres.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: The spleen is larger than usual. The spleen is an organ on the left side of your abdomen that helps filter blood.
entries.clinical_context: Measured on imaging, often reported in centimetres.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Lymph nodes are larger than usual. Lymph nodes are small glands that are part of your immune system.
entries.clinical_context: Described by location and size on imaging or examination.

entries.label: DESCRIPTOR
entries.plain_definition: Something noticed on a scan or test that was not what the test was looking for.
entries.clinical_context: Very common on imaging reports. Often not related to the reason for the test.

entries.label: DESCRIPTOR
entries.plain_definition: Nothing unusual was seen. In a report, this means the area looked as expected.
entries.clinical_context: A standard phrase in radiology reports. It is a normal result.

entries.label: SYMPTOM
entries.plain_definition: A body temperature that is higher than normal.
entries.clinical_context: Commonly understood term; not flagged for explanation.

entries.label: SYMPTOM
entries.plain_definition: Pain in the head.
entries.clinical_context: Commonly understood term; not flagged for explanation.

entries.label: TEST
entries.plain_definition: A measure of the force of blood pushing against the walls of your blood vessels.
entries.clinical_context: Commonly understood term; not flagged for explanation.

entries.label: SYMPTOM
entries.plain_definition: A sudden forceful release of air from the lungs.
entries.clinical_context: Commonly understood term; not flagged for explanation.

entries.label: SYMPTOM
entries.plain_definition: Feeling sick to your stomach, as if you might vomit.
entries.clinical_context: Commonly understood term; not flagged for explanation.

entries.label: DESCRIPTOR
entries.plain_definition: In lung imaging, consolidation is an area of increased lung opacity that occurs when air in the alveoli is replaced by fluid or other material. It describes an imaging appearance and does not by itself identify the underlying cause.
entries.clinical_context: Chest radiographs and chest CT reports; interpreted alongside the clinical presentation and other imaging findings.
entries.source_citation: Fleischner Society: Glossary of Terms for Thoracic Imaging (2024) — 'Consolidation'

entries.label: DESCRIPTOR
entries.plain_definition: Relating to or involving the kidneys.
entries.clinical_context: Used as an anatomical or functional descriptor in clinical notes, laboratory reports, imaging reports, and diagnoses involving the kidneys.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: In a spinal context, canal stenosis is narrowing of the spinal canal, which may reduce space available for the spinal cord or spinal nerve roots. The affected region and clinical significance depend on the location and degree of narrowing.
entries.clinical_context: Usually appears in cervical or lumbar spine MRI/CT reports and orthopedic, neurosurgical, or neurology notes. Read with the stated spinal level and whether central canal, lateral recess, or neural foraminal narrowing is described.

entries.label: DESCRIPTOR
entries.plain_definition: Relating to the mediastinum, the central compartment of the chest between the lungs that contains the heart and major blood vessels, trachea, esophagus, thymus, and lymph nodes.
entries.clinical_context: Used in chest imaging and thoracic clinical documentation to describe anatomy or findings, such as mediastinal lymph nodes, masses, widening, or pleural structures.
entries.source_citation: Cambridge Dictionary — 'Mediastinal'; anatomy cross-checked against NLM MeSH — 'Mediastinum'

entries.label: ANATOMY
entries.plain_definition: The narrowed portion of the femur between the femoral head and the trochanters, connecting the head of the femur to its shaft.
entries.clinical_context: Hip radiographs, CT/MRI reports, orthopedic notes, bone-density assessment, and descriptions of femoral-neck fractures.
entries.source_citation: National Library of Medicine MeSH — 'Femur Neck'

entries.label: DESCRIPTOR
entries.plain_definition: Relating to an antrum; in gastric clinical documentation, specifically relating to the pyloric antrum, the distal region of the stomach extending toward the pylorus.
entries.clinical_context: Upper endoscopy, gastric biopsy and pathology reports, and gastrointestinal imaging; examples include antral mucosa, antral gastritis, and antral biopsy.
entries.source_citation: National Library of Medicine MeSH — 'Pyloric Antrum'

entries.label: DESCRIPTOR
entries.plain_definition: Afebrile means without fever at the time of clinical assessment.
entries.clinical_context: Triage vitals, physical examinations, nursing notes, and progress notes.
entries.source_citation: Direct authoritative medical dictionary or clinical glossary reference required

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Scarring of the liver. The scar tissue takes the place of healthy liver tissue and cannot do the liver's usual work.
entries.clinical_context: Usually described on imaging or a liver biopsy, often alongside liver blood test results.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Inflammation of the liver. It can have several causes, including viruses.
entries.clinical_context: Often named by type or cause, for example hepatitis B or hepatitis C. Liver blood tests are usually reported alongside.

entries.label: SYMPTOM
entries.plain_definition: A yellow color of the skin or the whites of the eyes. It happens when a yellow substance called bilirubin builds up in the body.
entries.clinical_context: Noted on examination, often reported with a bilirubin blood test result.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: A yellow substance produced when the body breaks down old red blood cells. The liver processes it so it can leave the body.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in a liver function panel, sometimes as total and direct bilirubin. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Inflammation of the pancreas, a gland behind the stomach that helps digest food and control blood sugar.
entries.clinical_context: Described as acute (sudden) or chronic (long-term). Often reported with lipase or amylase blood test results.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A kidney cyst is a fluid-filled sac in the kidney. Simple kidney cysts are often harmless and become more common with age.
entries.clinical_context: Usually described from imaging, such as ultrasound, CT, or MRI; reports may note the cyst’s size and whether it appears simple or complex.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: An infection in the parts of the body that make and carry urine, such as the bladder or the kidneys.
entries.clinical_context: Usually found with a urine test or a urine culture.

entries.label: DESCRIPTOR
entries.plain_definition: Enlarged prostate describes an increase in the size or volume of the prostate gland. Causes may include benign prostatic hyperplasia, inflammation, malignancy, or other structural changes.
entries.clinical_context: Urology notes, digital rectal examination, ultrasound or other imaging reports, and diagnostic lists.
entries.source_citation: NCBI Bookshelf (supplied source lead; ensure it supports the broader descriptive definition)

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A type of irregular heartbeat. The upper chambers of the heart beat out of step with the lower chambers, often faster than usual.
entries.clinical_context: Seen on an ECG (also written EKG). Often shortened to AF or AFib.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: The heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs. It does not mean the heart has stopped.
entries.clinical_context: May be described as left-sided or right-sided. Often reported alongside an echocardiogram result such as ejection fraction.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A disease of the heart muscle that makes it larger, thicker, or stiffer than usual.
entries.clinical_context: Usually named by type, for example dilated or hypertrophic. Often seen on an echocardiogram.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A sticky substance called plaque builds up inside the arteries and makes them narrower.
entries.clinical_context: Often seen on imaging as plaque or calcium in the walls of blood vessels.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A bulge or ballooning in the wall of an artery.
entries.clinical_context: Usually described by its location, such as the aorta or a brain artery, and by its size.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A blood clot in a vein deep inside the body, most often in the leg.
entries.clinical_context: Usually found with an ultrasound scan of the leg veins. Often shortened to DVT.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A blockage in a blood vessel in the lungs, usually caused by a blood clot that has travelled there.
entries.clinical_context: Usually found on a CT scan of the chest. Often shortened to PE.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: An infection in one or both lungs that makes the tiny air sacs fill with fluid or pus.
entries.clinical_context: Often seen on a chest X-ray and described by the part of the lung involved.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Damage to the tiny air sacs in the lungs, so they do not stretch and empty the way they normally would. It is one type of COPD.
entries.clinical_context: Often described on a chest CT scan, sometimes as mild, moderate, or severe.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A group of long-term lung diseases that make it hard to breathe air in and out. Emphysema and chronic bronchitis are two kinds.
entries.clinical_context: Short for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Usually measured with breathing tests (spirometry).

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Inflammation of the bronchial tubes, the airways that carry air to the lungs. It commonly causes a cough that may bring up mucus.
entries.clinical_context: Often described as acute (short-term) or chronic (long-term); symptoms and duration vary by type.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A long-term lung condition. The airways can swell and get narrow, which makes it harder to breathe at times.
entries.clinical_context: Usually noted in the medical history. Breathing test results may be reported alongside.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Blood sugar levels that are higher than usual, but not high enough to be called diabetes.
entries.clinical_context: Based on blood tests such as HbA1c or fasting blood sugar.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A higher than usual level of sugar (glucose) in the blood.
entries.clinical_context: Seen on a blood glucose test.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A lower than usual level of sugar (glucose) in the blood.
entries.clinical_context: Seen on a blood glucose test.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Iron deficiency is a state in which the body’s available iron stores are insufficient to meet physiological needs. It can occur before, or alongside, iron-deficiency anemia.
entries.clinical_context: Hematology notes, ferritin and transferrin-saturation results, and diagnostic lists.
entries.source_citation: NLM MeSH (supplied source lead; direct support pending verification)

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: The body does not have enough vitamin D. Vitamin D helps the body take in calcium, which keeps bones strong.
entries.clinical_context: Measured with a vitamin D blood test, often reported as 25-hydroxy vitamin D.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Vitamin B12 deficiency occurs when the body does not have enough vitamin B12 to meet its needs. It can affect blood-cell formation and neurological function and may be present before macrocytic anemia or neurological symptoms become apparent.
entries.clinical_context: Diagnosis lists, hematology and neurology notes, nutritional assessment, and B12-related laboratory workups.
entries.source_citation: NCBI Bookshelf (supplied source lead; direct support pending verification)

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Hyponatremia is a low concentration of sodium in the blood. A commonly used threshold is serum sodium below 135 mEq/L, interpreted in the clinical context.
entries.clinical_context: Diagnosis lists, internal medicine notes, electrolyte panels, and inpatient assessments.
entries.source_citation: NCBI Bookshelf (supplied source lead; direct support pending verification)

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Hypokalemia is a low concentration of potassium in the blood. A commonly used threshold is serum potassium below 3.5 mEq/L, interpreted with the laboratory reference range and clinical context.
entries.clinical_context: Diagnosis lists, metabolic panels, cardiology notes, and internal medicine assessments.
entries.source_citation: NCBI Bookshelf (supplied source lead; direct support pending verification)

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A type of inflammatory arthritis caused by uric acid crystals forming in joints. It can cause sudden pain, swelling, and redness.
entries.clinical_context: Often reported with a uric acid blood test. It commonly affects the big toe.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: The thyroid gland makes more thyroid hormone than the body needs. Also called an overactive thyroid.
entries.clinical_context: Usually found with thyroid blood tests such as TSH and T4.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A goiter is an enlargement of the thyroid gland. It may occur when thyroid hormone levels are normal, elevated, or decreased.
entries.clinical_context: Neck examination, thyroid ultrasound, endocrine notes, and diagnostic lists.
entries.source_citation: NCBI Bookshelf (supplied source lead; direct support pending verification)

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Wear-and-tear arthritis. The smooth tissue (cartilage) that covers the ends of the bones in a joint breaks down.
entries.clinical_context: Often seen on X-rays of the knees, hips, hands, or spine.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: A sideways curve of the spine.
entries.clinical_context: Measured on an X-ray as an angle in degrees.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: One of the soft cushions between the bones of the spine has pushed out of its usual place.
entries.clinical_context: Seen on MRI or CT and described by its level in the spine, for example L4-L5.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Narrowing of the space inside the spine, which can press on the nerves or the spinal cord.
entries.clinical_context: Seen on MRI or CT, described by its level in the spine and as mild, moderate, or severe.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Diverticulosis is a condition characterized by the presence of small pouches called diverticula in the wall of the digestive tract, most commonly the colon. It is often asymptomatic and is distinct from diverticulitis, which involves inflammation of diverticula.
entries.clinical_context: Colonoscopy reports, abdominal CT findings, gastroenterology notes, and diagnosis lists.
entries.source_citation: NCBI Bookshelf (supplied source lead; direct support pending verification)

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Part of an organ or tissue bulges through a weak spot in a muscle wall, most often in the belly or groin.
entries.clinical_context: Usually named by location, for example inguinal (groin) or umbilical (belly button).

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Swollen veins around the anus or in the lower part of the rectum.
entries.clinical_context: Noted on examination or during a colonoscopy. Also called piles.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Small extra growths of tissue on the inside wall of the large intestine (colon).
entries.clinical_context: Found during a colonoscopy. Reports give the number and size, and removed polyps are usually sent to a lab for testing.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Growths made of muscle and other tissue in or around the wall of the uterus (womb). They are usually noncancerous.
entries.clinical_context: Seen on ultrasound or MRI, with the number and size described.

entries.label: DISEASE
entries.plain_definition: Fluid-filled sacs in or on an ovary. They are common and often form as part of the normal monthly cycle.
entries.clinical_context: Usually seen on a pelvic ultrasound, with the size given.

entries.label: TEST
entries.plain_definition: A group of blood measurements that counts blood cells and measures features such as hemoglobin and hematocrit.
entries.clinical_context: One of the most common blood tests. Results list each cell type with its own reference range.

entries.label: TEST
entries.plain_definition: A laboratory measurement that quantifies the number of white blood cells in a specified volume of blood.
entries.clinical_context: Complete blood count (CBC) and hematology reports.
entries.source_citation: NLM MeSH (supplied source lead; direct support pending verification)

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: The number of red blood cells in the blood. Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in a complete blood count (CBC). Reference ranges vary by lab.
entries.source_citation: MedlinePlus Medical Tests - 'Red Blood Cell (RBC) Count'

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: Small blood cells that help the blood clot and stop bleeding. A blood test counts how many are in the blood.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in a complete blood count (CBC) as the platelet count. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: The share of the blood that is made up of red blood cells, given as a percentage.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in a complete blood count (CBC), often shortened to Hct. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: The average size of the red blood cells.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in a complete blood count (CBC). Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: TEST
entries.plain_definition: A blood test that measures how quickly red blood cells settle to the bottom of a tube. It is a general check for inflammation in the body.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in millimetres per hour (mm/hr). Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: TEST
entries.plain_definition: A group of blood tests that measure substances made or handled by the liver, such as albumin, bilirubin, and liver enzymes.
entries.clinical_context: Also called a liver panel. Each result has its own reference range.

entries.label: TEST
entries.plain_definition: A quantitative laboratory measurement of albumin concentration in a serum or plasma sample.
entries.clinical_context: Comprehensive metabolic panel or hepatic-function testing.
entries.source_citation: NLM MeSH (supplied source lead; direct support pending verification)

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: An enzyme found throughout the body, with higher amounts in the liver, bile ducts, and bones.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in a liver function panel, often shortened to ALP. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: An enzyme found mainly in the liver and bile ducts.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in a liver function panel, often shortened to GGT. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: A waste product formed when the body breaks down protein. The kidneys remove it from the blood.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in a kidney function or metabolic panel, often shortened to BUN. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: A waste product made when the body breaks down substances called purines. The kidneys normally remove it in urine.
entries.clinical_context: Measured in blood or urine. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: An electrolyte (mineral) that helps regulate the body’s fluid balance and supports nerve and muscle function.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in an electrolyte or metabolic panel, often shortened to Na. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: An electrolyte (mineral) needed for cells, nerves, muscles, and normal heart rhythm to work properly.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in an electrolyte or metabolic panel, often shortened to K. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: An electrolyte (mineral) that helps maintain fluid balance and the body’s acid-base balance.
entries.clinical_context: Reported in an electrolyte or metabolic panel, often shortened to Cl. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: TEST
entries.plain_definition: A laboratory measurement of the concentration of unbound triiodothyronine in the blood. It may be used with other thyroid tests to assess thyroid function.
entries.clinical_context: Thyroid function panels and endocrine laboratory reports.
entries.source_citation: NLM MeSH (supplied source lead; verify free-T3-specific coverage)

entries.label: TEST
entries.plain_definition: A laboratory measurement of the concentration of unbound thyroxine in the blood. It is often interpreted alongside thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) to assess thyroid function.
entries.clinical_context: Thyroid function panels and endocrine laboratory reports.
entries.source_citation: NLM MeSH (supplied source lead; verify free-T4-specific coverage)

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: A protein that stores iron in the body. A blood test measures it to check how much iron the body has stored.
entries.clinical_context: Often reported with other iron tests. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: A mineral the body needs to make hemoglobin, the part of red blood cells that carries oxygen. Iron tests measure how much is in the blood.
entries.clinical_context: Often reported with ferritin and other iron tests. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: TEST
entries.plain_definition: A quantitative laboratory measurement of total cobalamin concentration in a serum or plasma sample.
entries.clinical_context: Nutritional panels and evaluation of anemia or suspected vitamin B12 deficiency.
entries.source_citation: NLM MeSH (supplied source lead; verify that it supports the laboratory-test concept)

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: Folate is a B vitamin that helps the body make healthy new cells.
entries.clinical_context: May appear as a measured nutrient in blood testing when folate deficiency is being assessed.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: A protein made by the liver when there is inflammation in the body. A blood test measures how much is in the blood.
entries.clinical_context: Often shortened to CRP. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: A protein found in heart muscle cells. A blood test measures how much is in the blood.
entries.clinical_context: Often measured more than once, a few hours apart. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: A natriuretic peptide hormone produced and released mainly by cardiac ventricular muscle cells in response to increased wall stress and stretch.
entries.clinical_context: Cardiology and heart-failure documentation; may be measured as a blood biomarker in assessment of suspected or known heart failure.

entries.label: BIOMARKER
entries.plain_definition: A protein made by the prostate, a gland in the male body. A blood test measures how much is in the blood.
entries.clinical_context: Often shortened to PSA. Reference ranges vary by lab.

entries.label: TEST
entries.plain_definition: A laboratory measurement of glucose concentration in blood collected after a fasting period, typically at least 8 hours without caloric intake.
entries.clinical_context: Routine screening, endocrine laboratory reports, and assessment or monitoring of diabetes.

entries.label: TEST
entries.plain_definition: A microbiological laboratory test that detects and identifies microorganisms growing in a urine sample. A positive result must be interpreted alongside the organism, colony count where applicable, sample quality, symptoms, and clinical context; it does not by itself establish a symptomatic urinary tract infection.
entries.clinical_context: Clinical microbiology reports and investigations for suspected urinary tract infection.

entries.label: ANATOMY
entries.plain_definition: A solid concretion, commonly formed from mineral salts, within an organ, duct, or body passage. The specific clinical meaning depends on anatomical location, such as a renal, ureteric, or gallbladder calculus.
entries.clinical_context: Ultrasound, CT, and other imaging reports across specialties; may occur in urinary, biliary, salivary, or other anatomical contexts.
